_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. status: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship / corroborated by reference works, citation in note), 'decided' (project style call, e.g. standard pinyin or a fixed convention), 'provisional' (a romanization of mine not found attested; the builder appends a visible marker). Sections render as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored.

黄慕兰.note: The author. Name taken in 1926 on joining the revolution (慕兰, ‘admiring Mulan’); the book’s title form.

黄彰定.note: The author’s birth and school name; style name Shuyi (淑仪). Corroborated by Chinese biographies.

黄定慧.note: A later name the author adopted in 1932; the form under which she is widely cited and by which the book’s photographs caption her.

谭嗣同.note: 1865–1898; Liuyang reformer, one of the ‘Six Gentlemen’ of 1898.

唐才常.note: 1867–1900; Liuyang reformer, with Tan Sitong the ‘Two Heroes of Liuyang.’

欧阳中鹄.note: 1849–1911; Liuyang Confucian scholar, teacher of Tan and Tang.

詹天佑.note: 1861–1919 (Jeme Tien Yow); pioneering railway engineer of the Beijing–Zhangjiakou line.

花木兰.note: Legendary woman warrior of the ‘Ballad of Mulan’; source of the author’s name.

何香凝.note: Wife of Liao Zhongkai; Kuomintang left-wing leader.

陈潭秋.note: 1896–1943; CCP founding member; the author’s leader in the Jiangxi underground.

杜韫章.note: Original name of Zhang Yun (章蕴, 1905–1995); the source glosses the identity inline.

李子芬.note: Standard pinyin; the CYL organizer who recruited the author.

袁溥之.note: d. 1994; Northern Expedition comrade of the author.

张笃和.note: Standard pinyin of a comrade of the author’s Wuhan years.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976; then the real director of the Party’s underground work in Shanghai; the author’s superior.

陈独秀.note: 1879–1942; first general secretary of the CCP, removed at the August Seventh Conference of 1927.

李一纯.note: Wife of Li Lisan; standard pinyin.

贺昌.note: 1906–1935; the author’s second husband; killed covering the Long March rearguard.

饶漱石.note: 1903–1975; later condemned in the 1954 Gao–Rao affair.

向忠发.note: 1880–1931; figurehead general secretary of the CCP from 1928.

吴德峰.note: Director of the Central Liaison Bureau.

徐虔直.note: Wife of Chen Tanqiu; romanization of 徐虑直 not found attested.

谢冰莹.note: 1906–2000; writer, author of Diary of a Woman Soldier; Whampoa 6th-class woman cadet.

胡兰畦.note: 1901–1994; writer, author of In Prison; Whampoa 6th-class woman cadet.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944; foreign minister of the Wuhan Nationalist government; conventional English form retained.

孙传芳.note: Warlord of the five southeastern provinces.

鲍罗廷.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), Comintern adviser to the Kuomintang at Wuhan.

沈定一.note: 1883–1928; early Communist; father of Shen Jianlong.

沈剑龙.note: First husband of Yang Zhihua; son of Shen Dingyi.

夏斗寅.note: Northern Expedition officer who mutinied against the Communists in May 1927.

许克祥.note: Launched the Changsha “Horse Day” coup, 21 May 1927.

耿丹.note: Styled Zhongzhao; deputy commander of the 15th Army; husband of Zhang Duhe.

赵畹华.note: Standard pinyin; the author’s Wuhan-years comrade.

汪华贞.note: Director of the Institute for Reforming New People at Wuhan.

刘少文.note: Subject of Appendix III; interpreter at the 1927 Wuhan reception.

江一平.note: Prominent Shanghai lawyer of the 1920s–30s; son-in-law of the magnate Yu Qiaqing. Assigned as the author’s duty defense lawyer in her 1929 mill-strike trial.

虞洽卿.note: Powerful Ningbo-born comprador and business magnate of Republican Shanghai.

李维汉.note: Alias Luo Mai (罗迈). Central Committee member and secretary of the Jiangsu Provincial Committee about 1929; a senior Party organizer.

王明.note: Chen Shaoyu; leader of the Moscow-trained ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and of the third ‘Left’ line (1931–35). Here still an obscure Red Flag reporter.

夏征农.note: Veteran Communist and writer; a member of the Central Advisory Commission in the 1980s.

聂荣臻.note: Later a marshal of the People’s Republic; in 1929–30 in charge of military work under the Guangdong Provincial Committee / Southern Bureau.

柯麟.note: Communist doctor who ran a Shanghai clinic (the Dasheng Clinic) as an underground liaison cover.

李强.note: Builder of the Party’s first wireless sets and secret radio stations; later PRC Minister of Foreign Trade.

张瑞华.note: Nie Rongzhen’s wife and a Party worker.

熊瑾玎.note: Manager of the Party Central’s clandestine finances in Shanghai.

贺平.note: The author’s second son, by He Chang, born March 1930 in Hong Kong; given to Lu Biao to raise and renamed Lu Ziping, later Lu Ping (卢平).

卢彪.note: Successor to He Chang as Southern Bureau (Guangdong Provincial Committee) secretary; adoptive father of the author’s son He Ping.

何葆贞.note: Liu Shaoqi’s wife (also written He Baozhen / He Bao’e), a Party worker and the author’s former Wuhan colleague; martyred 1934.

彭真.note: Later a top Party leader and mayor of Beijing; here Tianjin municipal committee secretary, arrested about this time.

薄一波.note: Later a vice-premier and Party elder; here Beiping municipal committee secretary.

陈复.note: A Northern Bureau leader arrested with the failed 1930 insurrections. The memoir calls him propaganda head; scholarship makes him the Bureau’s secretary-general.

任弼时.note: A principal Party and Youth League leader, later one of the ‘Five Secretaries’ of the Central Secretariat.

米夫.note: Pavel Mif, Comintern representative who engineered the Fourth Plenum of January 1931 that raised Wang Ming.

秦邦宪.note: Better known as Bo Gu (博古); one of the ‘28 Bolsheviks’ and de facto Party leader 1931–35.

张闻天.note: Alias Luo Fu (洛甫); a ‘28 Bolshevik’ who became general secretary after the Zunyi Conference.

王稼祥.note: Party and military leader; a supporter of Mao at the Zunyi Conference.

陈毅.note: Later a marshal and foreign minister of the People’s Republic.

毛泽覃.note: Mao Zedong’s youngest brother; killed in 1935.

戴晓云.note: New secretary of the Mutual Aid General Association from the winter of 1930; romanization by pinyin.

陈赓.note: Whampoa graduate and head of the intelligence (2nd) section of the Party’s Special Branch; later a PLA general.

谭延闿.note: Hunan military governor and Nationalist elder; first president of the Executive Yuan; signed the Wuhan order expelling Chiang in April 1927.

黄兴.note: Revolutionary leader and Sun Yat-sen’s chief military partner in the 1911 Revolution.

蔡锷.note: Republican general who led the 1915–16 revolt against Yuan Shikai’s monarchy.

顾顺章.note: Head of the Party’s Special Branch whose 1931 defection to the Kuomintang gravely wrecked the Shanghai underground.

戚元德.note: Wu Defeng’s wife and a Party worker skilled at persuasion; she talked the author into staying in Shanghai.

黄浩.note: Also styled Jingwen (静汰); staff officer of the Rescue Department, formerly of the Whampoa women’s corps. Romanization by pinyin.

朱伯琛.note: Secretary of the Mutual Aid General Association; son of Zhu Jianfan, headmaster of the Zhounan Girls’ School. Romanization by pinyin.

陈志皋.note: Progressive Shanghai lawyer of the Haining Chen clan; recruited to defend arrested Communists, he later became the author’s husband.

陈元龙.note: The ‘Grand Councilor Chen’ of the Kangxi–Yongzheng era, ancestor of the Haining Chen clan.

陈其寿.note: Styled Jieqing (介卿); Chen Zhigao’s father, a retired judge of the criminal court of the Shanghai French Concession’s Mixed Court; the author’s adoptive father.

翁同龢.note: The Guangxu Emperor’s tutor, cashiered in 1898 during the Hundred Days’ Reform.

黄金荣.note: Green Gang boss and the sole Chinese chief inspector of the French Concession patrol house; Chiang Kai-shek was once his disciple.

沈钧儒.note: Jurist and patriotic democrat, later one of the ‘Seven Gentlemen’; Chen Zhigao’s teacher and elder cousin.

褚辅成.note: Patriotic democrat and educator, principal of the Shanghai College of Law.

施蛰存.note: Modernist writer and scholar; a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

戴望舒.note: Celebrated modernist poet (‘Rainy Alley’); a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

杜衡.note: Writer and critic (Su Wen); a schoolmate bailed out by Chen’s father.

周康文.note: CCP Central Propaganda Department cadre who organized the World and China Society.

孙晓村.note: Economist and democrat; later a vice-chairman of the CPPCC and of the China Democratic National Construction Association.

钱纳水.note: Head of the propaganda department of the Mutual Aid General Association. Romanization by pinyin.

赵韵逸.note: The young judge who tried Guan Xiangying’s case. Romanization by pinyin.

贝淞生.note: Manager of the Bank of China and a sworn friend of the elder Chen. Romanization by pinyin.

宛希先.note: Cousin of the author’s first husband Wan Xiyan; an early Jinggangshan leader wrongly killed in the anti-‘AB-tuan’ purge about 1930.

邓榕.note: Pen name Maomao (毛毛); Deng Xiaoping’s daughter and biographer.

曹炳生.note: A French-Concession Municipal Police interpreter, classmate and dormitory-mate of Chen Zhigao at Xuhui College; his unwitting talk of Xiang Zhongfa’s arrest tipped off the author. Assassinated early in the War of Resistance.

薛耕莘.note: A Chinese detective in the Shanghai French-Concession police who succeeded to Cao Bingsheng’s post; later a research fellow of the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History and a memoirist (1901–2007).

孙雪影.note: Cao Bingsheng’s widow, headmistress of the Bingsheng Primary School founded in his memory.

康生.note: Took charge of the Central Special Branch after Gu Shunzhang’s defection in 1931; later a Politburo member and a chief instigator of the Cultural Revolution (1898–1975).

王震.note: Red Army and PLA general, later Vice-President of the PRC (1908–1993).

张国焘.note: An early CCP leader who, during the Long March, split with the Central Committee over the line of march; later defected to the Kuomintang (1897–1979).

柳亚子.note: Poet and founder of the Southern Society (Nanshe); a friend of Chen Zhigao’s (1887–1958).

李一氓.note: Party veteran and writer; the author quotes his account of the ‘Wu Hao’ affair from the volume Pan Hannian in Shanghai (1903–1990).

董竹君.note: Founder of the Jinjiang restaurant and hotel in Shanghai and author of the memoir My One Century; earlier the wife of Xia Zhishi (1900–1997).

夏之时.note: A Sichuan military commander (‘Commander Xia’, 都督) of the 1911 Revolution era; Dong Zhujun’s first husband, from whom she was divorced (1887–1950).

吴湄.note: Proprietress of the Meilongzhen Restaurant in Shanghai.

文崇石.note: Author of an article in the New York Chinese-language paper Overseas Chinese Daily exposing the Gang of Four’s use of the ‘Wu Hao’ notices against Zhou Enlai.

张承宗.note: Head of the United Front Work Department of the CCP Shanghai Municipal Committee (1907–1991).

俞同芳.note: A noted Shanghai practitioner of Chinese medicine, called in to attend Chen Qishou.

陈宝璋.note: Chen Zhigao’s younger sister, then a student at the Sino-French College of Pharmacy.

陈寅谷.note: A younger brother of Chen Zhigao, a student at the Tongde Medical College who did battlefield relief in the 1932 fighting.

陈石君.note: A younger brother of Chen Zhigao, a student at the Tongde Medical College who did battlefield relief in the 1932 fighting.

陈胜年.note: Later named Peng Qing (彭清); a grandson of Chen Qishou, born just before the old man’s death.

巴和.note: A French lawyer in Shanghai, an old friend of Chen Qishou; he placed the counter-notice on behalf of ‘Zhou Shaoshan’. Chinese sources give only 倩和 (Baho); his name’s French original is not established.

周少山.note: A cover name of Zhou Enlai, used in the March 1932 counter-notice: the notice styled ‘Wu Hao’ as merely a former pen name of the private citizen ‘Zhou Shaoshan’, so that the ‘Wu Hao’ of the fake notice must be someone else.

国民党.note: Rendered ‘Kuomintang’ throughout (not ‘Nationalist Party’); the conventional English name.

粤汉铁路.note: Conventional English form of the Guangzhou–Hankou line.

互济会.note: Successor to the China Relief Society; the Party-led body for rescuing arrested comrades and relieving their families. Its leading arm is called the Mutual Aid General Association (互济总会).

世界与中国社.note: A progressive study body organized under the CCP Central Propaganda Department, publisher of the periodical The World and China.

内外棉.note: Naigaiwata Kaisha, the largest Japanese-owned cotton-spinning company in Shanghai; the author worked as an apprentice in its No. 13 Mill.

特科.note: The Central Special Branch, the Party’s clandestine intelligence and security service in Shanghai, headed by Zhou Enlai.

觉悟社.note: A progressive youth group founded in Tianjin in 1919; Zhou Enlai was a leading member, and his code name there, ‘Wu Hao’, later became a pen name.

中央特科.note: The CCP’s clandestine security and intelligence organ in the Shanghai underground; run by Kang Sheng after Gu Shunzhang’s defection.

红旗印刷所.note: The underground printing house, holding an open business licence, where the Party magazine Red Flag was secretly printed; wrecked by the police when Xiang Zhongfa turned traitor.

都城饭店.note: A French-run hotel in Shanghai (the Metropole, on Jiangxi Road), used by the central leaders as a bolt-hole on the night of Xiang Zhongfa’s defection.

东方饭店.note: A Shanghai hotel where Guan Xiangying was lodged after his release.

申江医院.note: An underground-Party hospital on Avenue Joffre, run by Party comrades, used to treat leaders and shelter them; the author hid there after her father’s death.

大光明电影院.note: A famous Shanghai cinema (the Grand Theatre).

永安公司.note: A leading Shanghai department store on Nanjing Road (Wing On).

祥生公司.note: A Shanghai taxi company (its English name was Johnson & Co.).

徐汇公学.note: The Jesuit Collège Saint-Ignace at Xujiahui, Shanghai; a strict Catholic mission school where Chen Zhigao and Cao Bingsheng were classmates.

锦江饭店.note: Dong Zhujun’s restaurant, later hotel, in Shanghai.

梅龙镇酒家.note: A well-known Shanghai restaurant run by Wu Mei.

中法药科大学.note: A Shanghai pharmacy college where Chen Baozhang studied.

十九路军.note: The Kuomintang army that resisted the Japanese attack on Shanghai in the January Twenty-eighth (1932) war.

华侨日报.note: A Chinese-language newspaper published in New York (the China Daily News).

上海.note: China’s largest city and the seat of the Party Central and its underground in this period.

香港.note: British colony; seat of the Party’s Southern Bureau.

天津.note: North China treaty port; seat of the Party’s Northern Bureau.

龙华.note: District in the southern outskirts of Shanghai; site of the Kuomintang Garrison Command’s prison and execution ground.

庐山.note: A mountain resort in Jiangxi where Chiang Kai-shek was staying.

瑞金.note: The seat of the Central Soviet in Jiangxi, capital of the Chinese Soviet Republic.

大连.note: A city in Liaoning; Guan Xiangying’s native region, site of his memorial statue.

延安.note: The Communist base in northern Shaanxi from 1937.

霞飞路.note: A main thoroughfare of the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Central Huaihai Road.

法大马路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession, today’s Jinling East Road; the address on the counter-notice.

秀才.note: Lowest degree-holder of the imperial examinations; left romanized.

优贡.note: ‘Excellent tribute student,’ a special examination distinction; left romanized.

临江仙.note: ‘The Immortal by the River,’ a fixed ci lyric-pattern; each part of the book opens with one.

伍豪.note: An alias of Zhou Enlai, from his code name in the Awakening Society; the pivot of the fake ‘renunciation’ notices and their rebuttal.

周公.note: An honorific for Zhou Enlai; literally ‘Duke of Zhou’, the revered Zhou-dynasty statesman, here used as a byname of respect.
